title: Private Backup Download and Restore Flow: Signed URLs for Logistics Exports
author: JensenCole5829
summary: A restore screen should reveal almost nothing until an authorized administrator requests a specific tenant backup. TL;DR: keep every archive private, confirm the selected object with HEAD, and issue a short-lived signed download URL from an admin-only backend route. The browser can then download from storage without making the application server relay a large archive. If an operator proceeds, copy the archive to a separate restore-staging key and audit that transition. For a logistics SaaS, I would use the same boundary for database backups and tenant-scoped product-image exports. Application authorization decides who may request an object; knowing its key is never enough. Infrai is worth testing for teams that want this storage leg beside other backend modules because one key covers 295 capabilities across 20 modules through one REST API. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. The supporting benefit is concrete: adding an adjacent backend capability does not require another SDK and credential integration. Convenience still cannot waive a retention or restore test. How should a signed backup download and restore flow work? Define five inputs: tenant ID, backup key, expected byte count, retention deadline, and administrator authorization. A passing path proves that the object exists before showing the restore action, its size matches the catalog, the URL expires, the download works without forwarding the Infrai API key, and another tenant cannot select it. Keep the catalog in the application database. Store tenant, immutable backup ID, object key, creation time, expected size, retention deadline, and restore state. This storage surface cannot search object metadata server-side, and list supports prefix filtering only, so storage listing is not a searchable backup history. Deletion deserves equal weight: a daily retention worker can find expired catalog rows, delete their private objects, and preserve audit events. The lifecycle minimum is one day, which cannot implement hourly expiry. There is also no object versioning or object lock; accidental overwrites are not recoverable through this surface, and WORM retention needs an external system. This is an explicit trade-off between a broad common contract and specialist retention controls. Run the experiment before choosing the adapter This Python probe calls the verified object HEAD route directly. Run it before the admin backend creates a signed URL. It uses an environment variable for the key, an explicit HTTP method, status checks, and bounded retries that honor Retry-After . import json import os import time from urllib.error import HTTPError from urllib.parse import quote from urllib.request import Request , urlopen url_template = " https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key} " url = url_template . format ( bucket = quote ( os . environ [ " BACKUP_BUCKET " ], safe = "" ), key = quote ( os . environ [ " BACKUP_OBJECT_KEY " ], safe = " / " ), ) for attempt in range ( 4 ): request = Request ( url , method = " GET " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' INFRAI_API_KEY ' ] } " }, ) try : with urlopen ( request , timeout = 15 ) as response : print ( json . dumps ( json . load ( response ), indent = 2 , sort_keys = True )) break except HTTPError as error : if error . code == 429 and attempt < 3 : retry_after = error . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) time . sleep ( float ( retry_after ) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt ) continue detail = error . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " , errors = " replace " ) raise RuntimeError ( f " storage HEAD returned { error . code } : { detail } " ) from error Compare the returned existence and size with the catalog before enabling the restore action. The positive case then passes only if the backend issues a bounded signed URL and the archive checksum matches after a non-production restore. Repeat with a non-admin token, a key owned by another tenant, and a deliberately incorrect catalog size; each negative case passes only when the backend refuses to issue a URL. No invented latency score belongs in this decision. Wire the private flow Resolve the backup ID with a tenant-scoped database query, perform the object HEAD check shown above, and compare existence and size with the catalog. Only then request a short-lived signed URL and return it. Server-to-server calls use Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY ; the browser request to the returned signed URL must not carry that header. A HEAD retry is read-only. For URL creation, back off on HTTP 429, honor Retry-After , and surface other 4xx details rather than disguising them as missing files. If the workflow needs an audited target, copy the selected backup to a restore-staging key. Make the application operation idempotent. The platform specifies Idempotency-Key and a 24-hour default deduplication window, but application state should still stop two operators launching the same restore. The risky case is writing a newer archive to an existing key. There is no If-Match conditional write, so use unique immutable keys and update the current-backup pointer through a database transaction or queue. Keep it boring. Never overwrite. Product-image exports need a separate retention decision. An export may reference immutable image keys and expire on its own schedule, while an image should remain until no active export references it. Put those relationships in application data rather than expecting metadata search. Compare direct providers fairly Use the same positive and negative tests for every adapter. The unified option covers R2, S3, OSS, and COS behind one contract. Direct Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba Cloud OSS, and Tencent Cloud COS integrations use their respective control planes. That is the meaningful trade-off: the unified surface reduces integration variety across covered vendors, while a direct provider is the better evaluation path when a specialist storage feature decides the architecture. Option Good evaluation fit Test or boundary first Unified REST API One contract across storage and other backend capabilities No versioning, object lock, If-Match , or automatic cross-region replication Amazon S3 Direct S3 ownership or specialist requirements Tenant isolation, expiry, retention, and restore through the native adapter Cloudflare R2 Direct R2 ownership Signed-download behavior under the same application contract Alibaba Cloud OSS Direct OSS ownership Required region, retention, and deletion behavior Tencent Cloud COS Direct COS ownership Restore evidence and operational ownership Google Cloud Storage and Backblaze B2 are outside Infrai's coverage. Use a direct integration or another abstraction when either is mandatory. A specialist or direct provider is also the better fit for WORM retention, recoverable versions, self-service browser-upload CORS configuration, automatic cross-region replication, or bulk cross-cloud migration. The decision rule is blunt. Choose Infrai only if the authorization and signed-download tests pass, daily-or-longer lifecycle granularity works, immutable keys plus application coordination cover concurrency, and no missing specialist feature is required. Otherwise retain the application contract and select the direct provider that meets the unmet requirement. Treat deletion and restore as one system Before launch, walk one archive through creation, cataloging, HEAD verification, signed download, optional staging copy, restore, and deletion. Audit tenant, backup ID, actor, timestamp, source key, staging key when used, and outcome. Confirm that an expired URL fails and that deleting a catalog record cannot silently orphan its object. A missing object should disable restore and open an investigation. A size mismatch should block it. A denied tenant lookup should disclose no storage detail. Retry rate limits with bounded exponential backoff, but require an operator to resolve authorization and integrity failures. Schedule restore drills, too. The useful output is evidence that the archive works with the current schema and application code, not a green upload metric. Revisit the provider decision when retention, geography, or compliance needs change. If this boundary fits, start with the private backup restore guide and keep tenant authorization in your application. Sources RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics FedRAMP Amazon S3 documentation Cloudflare R2 documentation Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation Tencent Cloud COS documentation Infrai storage multipart discovery

title: I Tested 5 Proxy Types for Web Scraping — Here's What Actually Matters
author: Vlad Oso
summary: Last month I rebuilt a scraping pipeline that had been limping along on a bargain-bin datacenter proxy plan. The symptoms were familiar to anyone who's done this at any scale: success rate hovering around 60%, CAPTCHAs on every third session, and a monthly bill that made no sense relative to the data we were actually collecting. So I did what any reasonable developer would do: I spent two weeks testing every proxy type I could get my hands on against the same set of targets, with the same code, and wrote down what actually happened. This post is the write-up. No affiliate nonsense, no "top 10 providers" list — just what each proxy type is, when it works, when it fails, and the code patterns that matter regardless of which type you pick. The Setup Test workload: product pages from a handful of mid-size e-commerce sites, a couple of search-heavy directories, and one notoriously aggressive social platform. Roughly 50k requests per proxy type, spread across a week, using Python + requests . Same headers, same throttling (2–4s between requests per host), same retry logic. The only variable was the proxy layer. Here's the baseline code everything else builds on: import requests PROXY = " http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080 " proxies = { " http " : PROXY , " https " : PROXY , } def fetch ( url : str ) -> requests . Response : return requests . get ( url , proxies = proxies , timeout = 30 , headers = { " User-Agent " : ( " Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) " " AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) " " Chrome/128.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 " ), " Accept-Language " : " en-US,en;q=0.9 " , }, ) If you're copy-pasting proxy examples from blog posts, stop here and internalize one thing: most scraping failures are not proxy failures . They're fingerprint failures, rate failures, or session failures that a better proxy happens to mask. Keep that in mind as we go through the types, because the marketing for each type will happily take credit for all three. 1. Datacenter Proxies What they are: IPs allocated to hosting providers and cloud ranges (AWS, Hetzner, OVH, and thousands of smaller hosts). Cheap, fast, and trivially identifiable — the ASN alone gives them away. Results: ~55–65% success on the e-commerce targets, near-zero on the social platform. Latency was excellent (often under 300ms to first byte). Cost per GB was the lowest of anything tested by a wide margin. When to use them: Targets with weak or no bot protection (public APIs, small sites, RSS-like endpoints) High-volume, low-value requests where a 40% failure rate is acceptable because retries are cheap Geo-checking and uptime monitoring, where you just need an IP in a country, not a trustworthy one When to avoid: Anything behind Cloudflare Bot Management, DataDome, PerimeterX, or Akamai in a strict configuration. You'll burn your retry budget and learn nothing. 2. Residential Proxies (Rotating) What they are: IPs belonging to real consumer ISPs, routed through devices on home connections. Sold by the GB, usually with per-request or timed rotation. Results: ~92–96% success on e-commerce, ~80% on the social platform with careful session handling. Latency varied wildly — 800ms on a good exit node, 4s+ on a bad one. This variance is the price of admission. The single biggest improvement in my whole test came from rotation strategy , not from switching providers. Two patterns matter: Per-request rotation — fresh IP every request. Good for stateless, high-parallelism workloads: import random import string def session_id () -> str : return "" . join ( random . choices ( string . ascii_lowercase + string . digits , k = 8 )) def rotating_proxy () -> dict : # Most rotating residential gateways encode the session in the username. # A new session ID = a new exit IP. user = f " customer- { session_id () } " proxy = f " http:// { user } :password@gateway.example.com:8080 " return { " http " : proxy , " https " : proxy } Sticky sessions — same IP for N minutes. Mandatory for anything with login state, carts, or multi-step flows: class StickySession : """ One exit IP per logical task; rotate only when the task ends or fails. """ def __init__ ( self , ttl_requests : int = 50 ): self . ttl = ttl_requests self . count = 0 self . session = self . _new_session () def _new_session ( self ) -> requests . Session : s = requests . Session () sid = session_id () proxy = f " http://customer- { sid } :password@gateway.example.com:8080 " s . proxies = { " http " : proxy , " https " : proxy } return s def get ( self , url : str , ** kw ) -> requests . Response : if self . count >= self . ttl : self . session = self . _new_session () self . count = 0 self . count += 1 return self . session . get ( url , timeout = 30 , ** kw ) Honest trade-off: you're paying per GB for traffic that transits someone's home connection. That makes residential the wrong tool for downloading large payloads, and the right tool when the cost of a blocked request (a missed price change, a dead account) exceeds the cost of the bandwidth. 3. Mobile Proxies What they are: IPs from carrier networks (4G/5G). The magic here is CGNAT: hundreds or thousands of real subscribers share a single public IP, so aggressive blocking hurts the site's real users — which means sites are very reluctant to block mobile IPs outright. Results: Highest success rate of the test (~97% even on the social platform). Also the slowest and most expensive per GB, typically 3–10× residential pricing. When to use them: Social platforms, account-adjacent automation, anywhere a block is catastrophic rather than merely annoying. When to avoid: Bulk scraping. You'll go bankrupt feeding a price monitor through mobile bandwidth. Also note that mobile IPs rotate on their own schedule (tower handoffs, NAT timeouts), so long sticky sessions are not guaranteed no matter what the sales page says. 4. ISP Proxies What they are: Datacenter-hosted IPs that are registered to consumer ISPs. You get the speed and stability of a datacenter connection with an ASN that looks residential. Typically sold per-IP, per-month rather than per-GB. Results: ~90% success on e-commerce, stable latency (~400ms), and — uniquely in this test — the same IPs stayed fast and unblocked for the entire week. No rotation lottery. When to use them: Long-running jobs against a fixed set of targets, monitoring tasks, anything where you want residential-grade trust with datacenter-grade predictability and a flat monthly bill. When to avoid: Workloads that need thousands of distinct IPs. Per-IP pricing means breadth costs money, and if you hammer one ISP IP hard enough, it will get flagged eventually — the pool you can fall back to is much smaller than a rotating residential pool. 5. Static (Dedicated) Proxies A quick taxonomy note, because vendors abuse these terms: "static" describes behavior (the IP doesn't change), not a network type. A static proxy can be a datacenter IP or an ISP IP that you keep for the duration of your plan. In my test setup, static ISP was the workhorse configuration for the monitoring jobs — one IP per target site, requests spread politely, zero surprises across two weeks. The general rule: rotating for breadth, static for depth. If a job revisits the same target repeatedly and failure has consequences, static wins. If a job fans out across many targets and individual failures are cheap, rotate. Detecting Blocks (and Not Lying to Yourself About It) The most dangerous scraping system is one that reports 100% success while quietly ingesting garbage. Sites defend themselves on a spectrum: Hard blocks: 403, 429, connection resets. Easy to detect, easy to handle. Soft blocks: HTTP 200 with a CAPTCHA page, a "verify you're human" interstitial, or an empty-but-valid HTML shell. This is where pipelines go to die. Your parser returns empty results and nobody notices for a week. Honeypots and poisoned data: 200 with subtly wrong data — prices off by a digit, shuffled listings, fake out-of-stock flags. Rare, but they exist specifically to corrupt datasets like yours. Detection needs to be structural, not status-code-based: BLOCK_MARKERS = ( " captcha " , " verify you are human " , " access denied " , " are you a robot " , " unusual traffic " , " px-captcha " , ) def classify ( resp : requests . Response , expected_selector_found : bool ) -> str : if resp . status_code in ( 403 , 429 , 503 ): return " hard_block " body = resp . text . lower () if any ( m in body for m in BLOCK_MARKERS ): return " soft_block " if resp . status_code == 200 and not expected_selector_found : return " suspect " # 200 but the data isn't there — treat as failure return " ok " Track these categories separately in your metrics. If your dashboard only shows HTTP status codes, you're flying blind. And the retry logic that ties it together — retry on a different IP for hard/soft blocks, back off on 429s, and never retry a poisoned response: import time def fetch_with_recovery ( url : str , task : StickySession , attempts : int = 4 ): for i in range ( attempts ): try : resp = task . get ( url ) except requests . RequestException : resp = None if resp is not None : verdict = classify ( resp , expected_selector_found = has_data ( resp )) if verdict == " ok " : return resp if verdict == " suspect " : # Possible honeypot — log it, don't ingest, don't blindly retry raise SuspiciousResponse ( url ) # Hard block, soft block, or network error: new exit IP, then back off task . session = task . _new_session () task . count = 0 time . sleep ( min ( 2 ** i , 30 )) raise BlockedError ( f " { url } failed after { attempts } attempts " ) Cost Optimization: Stop Burning Residential GB on JPEGs Per-GB pricing means every byte counts, and the default behavior of most scraping stacks is a bonfire. In my first pipeline version, over 60% of residential traffic was images, fonts, and CSS — assets I was never going to parse. The fixes, in order of impact: Block static assets. If you're parsing HTML, you need HTML. In requests this means not following asset URLs at all; in browser automation (Playwright/Selenium), intercept and abort image/font/media requests. This alone halved my bill. Route by target hardness. Send the easy 80% of targets through datacenter proxies at a fraction of the cost, and reserve residential for the hosts that actually block you. A simple per-host success-rate table in your code can automate this routing after a day of data. Cache aggressively at the URL level. Product pages rarely change minute-to-minute. A 15-minute in-memory cache on listing pages eliminated a third of my requests entirely. Compress and shrink. Send Accept-Encoding: gzip, br explicitly (some proxy gateways strip it), and use HEAD /conditional requests where the target supports ETags. Right-size sessions. Sticky sessions that live too long waste the "freshness" you're paying for; sessions that rotate too often waste connection setup and look bot-like. 10–30 minutes is the sweet spot for most of my workloads. After all five, the same crawl that cost me a painful amount in week one ran at roughly one third of the cost in week two — with a higher success rate, because blocked-target routing meant residential IPs were only spent where they mattered. The Summary Table Type Trust level Speed Pricing model Best for Datacenter Low Fastest Per IP / per GB (cheap) Weakly defended targets, monitoring Residential (rotating) High Variable Per GB General-purpose scraping, breadth Mobile Highest Slowest Per GB (expensive) Social platforms, high-stakes requests ISP High Fast + stable Per IP / month Long-running jobs, fixed targets Static (ISP/DC) Depends on base Stable Per IP / month Sessions, accounts, depth over breadth What I'd Do Differently Two lessons stuck. First, log the block taxonomy from day one — retrofitting detection onto a pipeline that assumed 200 = success cost me more time than the proxy testing itself. Second, match the proxy to the failure cost, not to the target's reputation. "This site is hard, use mobile" is worse advice than "this request is expensive to lose, use mobile." For the residential and static ISP portions of this test I used IPStation ($2.50/GB dynamic residential, $3.99/month static ISP, and the 200MB free trial was enough to validate the setup before spending anything) — but honestly, every pattern in this post is provider-agnostic. Pick any reputable vendor, steal the detection and routing code, and you'll get 90% of the benefit. The proxies were never the hard part. Knowing why a request failed — and what that failure should make your code do next — is the whole game. Questions or better war stories? Drop them in the comments — especially if you've caught a target serving poisoned data in the wild. I want to hear how you detected it.

title: Python Lazy Imports: How the New lazy Keyword Works in Python 3.15
author: Mahir Faysal
summary: Python 3.15 adds explicit lazy imports: write lazy import json (or lazy from pathlib import Path ) and Python won’t load the module until your code first uses that name. You keep all your imports neatly at the top of the file, but you only pay the loading cost for modules a particular run actually needs. In my test, a script that imported a slow module started in 0.50 seconds with a normal import and 0.00 seconds with lazy import , and the module loaded later, only when it was called. Lazy imports come from PEP 810 and are one of the biggest changes in Python 3.15.0, released on 9 October 2026. I tested everything below on Python 3.15.0rc3 (installed with uv python install 3.15 ), and pasted the real output, including the error messages. The behaviour matches the final release notes. Why imports slow Python down When Python imports a module, the What’s New in Python 3.15 guide explains, it must locate the file, read it from disk, compile it to bytecode and execute all its top-level code. For applications with deep dependency trees, that can take seconds, “even when most of the imported code is never actually used during a particular run.” Command-line tools feel this most. Typing mytool --help shouldn’t load your database driver, plotting library and HTTP client, but with normal imports at the top of the file, it does. Developers have worked around this for years: Moving import statements inside functions. Using importlib.import_module() on demand. Restructuring code to avoid importing heavy packages. They all work, but they scatter imports through the code and make it harder to see what a module depends on. The lazy keyword fixes that without moving anything. The syntax: lazy import and lazy from … import lazy goes in front of an ordinary import statement. Both forms work: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path lazy is a soft keyword , which means it’s only special at the start of an import statement. Existing code that uses lazy as a variable name keeps working; lazy = 5; print(lazy) printed 5 on 3.15. Older versions don’t understand the syntax at all. Running the same file on Python 3.14 gives: File "./app_lazy.py", line 2 lazy import heavy ^^^^^^ SyntaxError: invalid syntax So the keyword form is only for code that will run on 3.15 or later. There’s a compatible alternative later in this post. Measuring the startup difference To see the effect clearly, I made a fake “heavy” module that sleeps for half a second when it loads, standing in for a big library: # heavy.py import time print ( " [heavy] loading... " ) time . sleep ( 0.5 ) def report (): return " report ready " First, a normal import: # app_eager.py import time ; t = time . perf_counter () import heavy print ( f " started in { time . perf_counter () - t : . 2 f } s " ) [heavy] loading... started in 0.50s Now the lazy version, which also checks sys.modules (Python’s registry of loaded modules) before and after first use: # app_lazy.py import time ; t = time . perf_counter () lazy import heavy print ( f " started in { time . perf_counter () - t : . 2 f } s " ) import sys print ( " in sys.modules? " , " heavy " in sys . modules ) print ( heavy . report ()) print ( " in sys.modules? " , " heavy " in sys . modules ) started in 0.00s in sys.modules? False [heavy] loading... report ready in sys.modules? True The import line cost nothing. The module only loaded at heavy.report() , and from then on it’s a completely normal module. If a run never touches heavy , it never loads at all. What a lazy import actually creates Behind the scenes, a lazy import binds the name to a lightweight proxy object . The proxy type is available as types.LazyImportType , and sys.get_lazy_imports() tells you the current global mode: import types , sys lazy import heavy lazy from json import dumps print ( type ( globals ()[ " heavy " ]). __name__ , isinstance ( globals ()[ " heavy " ], types . LazyImportType )) print ( sys . get_lazy_imports ()) print ( dumps ({ " ok " : True })) print ( type ( globals ()[ " dumps " ]). __name__ ) lazy_import True normal {"ok": true} function I peeked through globals() on purpose, because simply writing heavy would trigger the load. After dumps() was first called, the name was replaced by the real function. The mode normal is the default: only imports marked lazy are lazy. Where lazy imports aren’t allowed The 3.15 documentation lists three restrictions, and each one gives a clear SyntaxError . I tried all of them. Inside a function (or class body): def f (): lazy import json SyntaxError: lazy import not allowed inside functions Inside try/except (or finally ): try : lazy import json except ImportError : pass SyntaxError: lazy import not allowed inside try/except blocks Star imports (and from __future__ imports): lazy from json import * SyntaxError: lazy from ... import * is not allowed The try/except rule makes sense once you think about it: a lazy import doesn’t run at that line, so an except ImportError around it could never catch anything. If you need an optional dependency with a fallback, keep using a normal import inside try . How errors show up with lazy imports Because nothing is loaded at the import line, a missing module isn’t reported there. The documentation says the exception is raised at the point of first use, with a traceback that includes both places. Here’s what that looks like: lazy import does_not_exist print ( " import line passed " ) does_not_exist . run () import line passed Traceback (most recent call last): File "./app_missing.py", line 1, in <module> lazy import does_not_exist ImportError: lazy import of 'does_not_exist' raised an exception during resolution The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception: Traceback (most recent call last): File "./app_missing.py", line 3, in <module> does_not_exist.run() ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'does_not_exist' The program printed “import line passed” before failing. That’s the main trade-off of lazy imports: typos in module names and missing dependencies surface later, possibly in a code path your tests don’t cover. Run your test suite with good coverage, and consider a quick smoke test that imports everything eagerly (see the global mode below). Making every import lazy: -X lazy_imports and PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS You can switch the behaviour on for a whole program without editing any source, using either the -X lazy_imports command-line option or the PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS environment variable. Both accept all (make all imports lazy by default) or normal (the default, respecting only the keyword). With this plain file: # app_all.py import heavy print ( " all-mode: started " ) print ( heavy . report ()) $ python3.15 -X lazy_imports=all app_all.py all-mode: started [heavy] loading... report ready $ PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS=all python3.15 app_all.py all-mode: started [heavy] loading... report ready The ordinary import heavy became lazy: “started” printed before the module loaded. This is a quick way to measure how much your app would gain before you change any code. Some libraries rely on side effects at import time (registering plugins, patching other modules), so test carefully before turning all on in production. You can also change the mode at runtime with sys.set_lazy_imports() and read it with sys.get_lazy_imports() . Choosing which modules are lazy with a filter For finer control, sys.set_lazy_imports_filter() takes a function that decides per import. It receives the importing module’s name, the imported module’s name and the fromlist , and returns True to allow lazy loading. Here only heavy is allowed to be lazy, and json is forced to load eagerly: import sys def only_heavy ( importing , imported , fromlist ): return imported == " heavy " sys . set_lazy_imports_filter ( only_heavy ) sys . set_lazy_imports ( " all " ) import heavy import json print ( " heavy loaded? " , " heavy " in sys . modules , " | json loaded? " , " json " in sys . modules ) heavy loaded? False | json loaded? True The documentation suggests a similar pattern for making only your own application’s modules lazy (for example, everything starting with myapp. ) while keeping third-party libraries eager. Supporting Python 3.14 and older: lazy_modules If your code must still run on older versions, you can’t use the keyword, because it’s a syntax error there. Instead, define __lazy_modules__ at the top of the module: a list of fully qualified module names. On 3.15, normal imports of those modules become lazy; on older versions the variable is just an unused list and the imports run eagerly as before. __lazy_modules__ = [ " heavy " ] import heavy print ( " compat: started " ) print ( heavy . report ()) compat: started [heavy] loading... report ready That’s the best of both worlds for libraries: faster startup on 3.15, no breakage on 3.14. A real-world example: a command-line tool Here’s the situation lazy imports were designed for. This small tool has two sub-commands. Only report needs the slow module, but with a normal import, version would pay for it too: # tool.py import sys lazy import heavy def main ( argv ): if argv [: 1 ] == [ " version " ]: print ( " tool 1.0 " ) elif argv [: 1 ] == [ " report " ]: print ( heavy . report ()) else : print ( " usage: tool.py [version|report] " ) main ( sys . argv [ 1 :]) I timed both commands from the shell: $ time python3.15 tool.py version tool 1.0 real 0.01s $ time python3.15 tool.py report [heavy] loading... report ready real 0.51s The version command never loads heavy , so it returns almost instantly. The report command loads it when it’s needed. The import still sits at the top of the file, where anyone reading the code can see every dependency. Lazy imports vs importing inside a function The traditional workaround is to put the import inside the function that needs it: import time , sys def make_report (): import heavy # old trick: import inside the function return heavy . report () t = time . perf_counter () print ( " started " , f " { time . perf_counter () - t : . 2 f } s " , " heavy " in sys . modules ) print ( make_report ()) started 0.00s False [heavy] loading... report ready It works on every Python version and gives the same startup saving, so it’s still a good choice for code that must support 3.14 and earlier. The downsides are readability and repetition: dependencies are hidden inside functions, and if three functions need the module, you write the import three times. With lazy import the dependency is declared once, at the top, and loaded once, on first use. There’s also importlib.util.LazyLoader , which has existed for years, but it needs several lines of setup code per module. The new keyword replaces that boilerplate for most everyday cases. How to measure your own import time Before optimising, find out which imports are actually slow. Python has had a built-in import profiler for years: python -X importtime your_script.py prints how long each module took to import (in microseconds), with nested imports indented. Sort by the cumulative column and the expensive ones stand out. Those are your best candidates for lazy . A rough checklist I’d follow: Run python3.15 -X importtime app.py 2> imports.txt and look for the biggest cumulative times. Try -X lazy_imports=all and time the startup again to see the upper limit of what you can gain. Mark the slow, rarely used imports with lazy , starting with ones only needed in one command or code path. Run your tests, and check that import-time side effects (such as plugin registration) still happen when needed. When lazy imports help (and when they don’t) They help most in command-line tools with many sub-commands, web apps with rarely used admin features, test suites where each test touches a few modules, and serverless functions where cold-start time costs money. They don’t help when every run uses every import anyway; you only move the cost later. They also won’t speed up code inside a hot loop, because after first use a lazily imported module is a normal module. They can surprise you when a module does something important at import time. If import myapp.plugins registers handlers, making it lazy means those handlers don’t exist until something touches myapp.plugins . Keep such imports eager. For file and path checks at startup, which often go hand in hand with deciding what to load, my guide to checking if a file exists in Python covers pathlib , which itself is a good candidate for lazy from pathlib import Path in small scripts. FAQ What is a lazy import in Python? A lazy import delays loading a module until the imported name is first used. In Python 3.15 you write lazy import module or lazy from module import name , and Python binds a lightweight proxy that loads the real module on first access. Which Python version supports the lazy keyword? Python 3.15 and later, released on 9 October 2026 (PEP 810). On Python 3.14 and earlier, lazy import is a SyntaxError . Use __lazy_modules__ if your code must run on both. Can I use lazy import inside a function? No. Lazy imports are only allowed at module level. Using lazy inside a function, class body or try / except / finally block raises a SyntaxError . A normal import inside a function is already effectively lazy. What happens if a lazily imported module doesn’t exist? The import line succeeds, and the error appears when you first use the name. Python raises an ImportError chained to the original ModuleNotFoundError , with a traceback showing both the import line and the line where you used it. How do I make all imports lazy? Run Python with -X lazy_imports=all or set the environment variable PYTHON_LAZY_IMPORTS=all . You can also call sys.set_lazy_imports("all") at runtime, and use sys.set_lazy_imports_filter() to exclude specific modules. Do lazy imports make my code faster? They make startup faster when some imports aren’t needed on every run. They don’t speed up code that runs after the module is loaded, and if every import is used on every run, the total time stays about the same. Is lazy a reserved word now? No. It’s a soft keyword, only special at the start of an import statement. Variables named lazy still work. Originally published on mfaysal.com . title: Six SaaS metric formulas and the edge cases that break them
author: 牛云鹏
summary: Every SaaS metric calculator is five lines of arithmetic. The bugs are all in the edges. I wrote six of them — LTV:CAC, CAC payback, quick ratio, MRR/ARR, churn rate and runway — and wrote the tests before the UI. Below are the cases that return an answer which looks completely reasonable and is completely wrong. They are worth knowing even if you never build a calculator, because the same arithmetic sits inside every spreadsheet that reports these numbers. 1. Zero churn makes LTV infinite Average customer lifetime is 100 / monthlyChurnPct . At zero churn that is Infinity , so LTV is Infinity , so the LTV:CAC ratio is Infinity . Nothing throws. The UI renders a number. The number is unbeatable. const lifetimeMonths = churnPct <= 0 ? null : 100 / churnPct const ltv = lifetimeMonths === null ? null : arpu * grossMargin * lifetimeMonths Return null and render "unbounded" with a note that real cohorts always churn eventually. An explicit null beats a helpful default, because a default can be silently summed into a total while null has to be handled. Same trap on the other side: CAC = 0 makes the ratio infinite. Zero CAC is never true, it means the denominator was not filled in. 2. Annual contracts booked as one month A $1,200 annual plan is $100 of MRR. Booking the cash when it lands gives you this: March MRR jumps by $1,200 April MRR falls by $1,100 relative to March Every chart downstream — net new MRR, growth rate, quick ratio — inherits the spike and the crash The twelve-fold error is not a rounding problem, it is a definition problem: MRR is a rate, not a receipt. Amortise the contract across its term before it reaches any metric. const mrr = billingPeriod === ' annual ' ? planPrice / 12 : planPrice 3. LTV on revenue instead of gross profit The 3x rule of thumb assumes gross profit. Using revenue inflates LTV by 1 / grossMargin — at an 80% margin that is 25% too high, at 50% it is double. // wrong: compares revenue to a cost const ltv = arpu * lifetimeMonths // right: compares profit to a cost const ltv = arpu * grossMargin * lifetimeMonths This one is nasty because the result still looks like a number. At a 70% margin a business at 2.1x looks like 3.0x, and the conclusion flips from "underinvesting" to "healthy". 4. CAC payback without the margin const paybackMonths = cac / ( arpu * grossMargin ) Drop grossMargin and payback shrinks by the margin: at 80% a real 6.25-month payback reports as 5.0. The rule of thumb is "under 12 months", so a 15-month payback reported as 12 sits exactly on the boundary and passes. 5. Quick ratio when nothing churned const quickRatio = mrrLost === 0 ? null : mrrGained / mrrLost A month with no churn is either a tiny base or a data problem. Rendering Infinity makes it indistinguishable from a genuinely excellent month, and it will be copied into a board deck. 6. Money is not a float 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 . It does not matter at these magnitudes until you start summing and comparing — and then paybackMonths <= 12 is false for what a human computes as 12.0. For a single calculation, round only at the point of display. If you are summing rows, store integer cents. const round = ( n : number , dp = 2 ) => Math . round ( n * 10 ** dp ) / 10 ** dp The general rule Every one of these is the same bug wearing a different hat: a missing value is not zero, and an unbounded value is not a large one. A calculator whose inputs are optional and whose outputs are numbers needs a third state. null in the model, an explicit "not enough information" in the UI. The alternative is a dashboard that is confidently wrong, which is worse than one that is visibly empty. I put these six into free, no-signup calculators — LTV:CAC , CAC payback , quick ratio , MRR & ARR , churn and runway . Every one shows its formula and its derivation, and the edge cases above are covered by tests rather than by hope.

title: Selling a paid Discord community on Gumroad? Your refunded buyers probably still have access
author: Pau Drudis
summary: A paid Discord is one of the easiest things to sell on Gumroad: a course community, a trading channel, a mod-support server. The usual setup goes like this: buyer pays, buyer pastes their license key into a bot, and the bot gives them a role. There are two quiet bugs in almost every version of that setup. Bug 1: success: true doesn't mean "paid" Gumroad's POST /v2/licenses/verify returns success: true for a key even after the purchase was refunded or charged back . You have to check the purchase flags yourself: function isActive ( p ) { if ( p . refunded || p . chargebacked || p . disputed ) return false ; if ( p . subscription_ended_at || p . subscription_cancelled_at || p . subscription_failed_at ) return false ; return true ; } If your bot only checks success , a buyer can pay, get the role, refund, and stay in your server indefinitely. Bug 2: Gumroad pings aren't signed To remove roles on refund, you'll use Gumroad's Ping (Settings → Advanced). But the ping is a plain form POST with no signature. Anyone who learns the URL can send sale_id=... and pretend. The fix is simple: treat the ping only as a "something changed" signal . Pull the sale ID out of it and re-fetch the real record: const r = await fetch ( `https://api.gumroad.com/v2/sales/ ${ saleId } ` , { headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${ process . env . GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN } ` } }); const { sale } = await r . json (); if ( isActive ( sale )) grantRole (); else revokeRole (); Also put a long random secret in the ping URL, and compare it with crypto.timingSafeEqual . Adding and removing the role With a bot that has Manage Roles , and whose own role sits above the roles it grants: const url = `https://discord.com/api/v10/guilds/ ${ GUILD } /members/ ${ userId } /roles/ ${ roleId } ` ; await fetch ( url , { method : ' PUT ' , headers : { Authorization : `Bot ${ BOT_TOKEN } ` } }); // grant await fetch ( url , { method : ' DELETE ' , headers : { Authorization : `Bot ${ BOT_TOKEN } ` } }); // revoke Two more things people miss Key sharing. Store sale_id → discord_id and refuse to link the same sale to a second account. Missed pings. Hosts restart, and pings get dropped. Run a nightly job that re-checks every linked sale and revokes anything inactive. Free check, or the full thing The refund-aware license check on its own is free and MIT licensed: gumroad-license-check . If you'd rather not wire up the rest yourself, the Gumroad → Discord Access Kit packages all of it: the ping endpoint, the linking form, one-key-per-account, the nightly reconcile and 12 tests, with zero dependencies.

title: Sephora Paid $1.2M for Ignoring Global Privacy Control. Check Your Site in CI
author: Louis Wright
summary: This article was written with AI assistance and reviewed before publishing. The demo site used in the examples is made up for this article. On August 24, 2022, California's Attorney General announced a $1.2 million settlement with Sephora. The allegations were simple: Sephora sold customers' personal information without telling them, and it failed to process opt-out requests sent through user-enabled global privacy controls such as the Global Privacy Control (GPC) [1]. On the same day, the office said it had sent notices to a number of other businesses over the same failure to process GPC opt-outs [1]. Nobody at Sephora had to click a button for that to happen. A shopper's browser sent a signal, the site did not act on it, and advertising tags kept loading. Almost three years later, in July 2025, the same office announced a $1.55 million settlement with Healthline.com, describing it at the time as the largest CCPA settlement to date. One of the allegations was that Healthline kept sharing data with some advertising third parties even for consumers who had opted out, and the announcement spelled out that businesses must honour opt-out requests, including those sent through GPC [2]. If you ship a site with a Meta Pixel, a TikTok Pixel or a LinkedIn Insight Tag on it, this is a frontend problem as much as a legal one. This post walks through what the signal actually is, what "honouring" it means in code, and how to catch the gaps in CI with an open-source CLI called gpc-warden. What GPC actually sends Global Privacy Control is a W3C specification. When a user turns it on, the browser does two things [3]: It adds a Sec-GPC: 1 request header to the requests it makes. It exposes navigator.globalPrivacyControl , a read-only boolean that tells your scripts whether that header was sent for the current top-level page. The spec also defines an optional support resource at /.well-known/gpc.json . Its gpc member must be true (the server intends to abide by GPC requests, at least as far as it is legally obliged to) or false , and an optional lastUpdate member holds a YYYY-MM-DD date [3]. A valid file looks like this: { "gpc" : true , "lastUpdate" : "2026-10-20" } California's own CCPA guidance lists the right to opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information "including via the GPC", and tells consumers they can submit an opt-out request through a user-enabled global privacy control [4]. So the header is not a hint. Under that guidance it is a request your site is expected to act on. Why sites get this wrong Reading a boolean is easy. The hard part is that most ad tags are pasted straight into a layout as a bare <script async src="..."> . A tag loaded like that runs on every page view, and there is no point at which your code gets to ask "did this visitor opt out?" before the pixel fires. Honouring GPC in a static or mostly static site comes down to two things: Some code has to read the signal: an inline script, a loader in your own JS bundle, an edge or serverless function that looks at Sec-GPC , or a consent management platform (CMP) configured to respect it. Every sale/share tag has to load in a way that code can stop: through that loader, or tagged so your CMP controls it (for example type="text/plain" plus a category attribute). Miss either one and the signal is effectively ignored, even if your privacy policy says otherwise. Checking a built site with gpc-warden gpc-warden is a zero-dependency Node.js CLI, library and GitHub Action that inspects the folder your build writes (Astro, Next.js output: 'export' , Eleventy, Hugo, Jekyll, Docusaurus, VitePress or plain HTML). It runs offline and checks: whether any inline script, local JS file or edge/serverless function in the build reads navigator.globalPrivacyControl or Sec-GPC ; whether advertising vendors that sell or share data (Meta, Google Ads, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, Pinterest, Snap, Microsoft, Criteo, Taboola and others) load unconditionally; whether /.well-known/gpc.json exists, is valid, and does not say false while sale/share tags are present; whether the privacy policy mentions GPC or opt-out preference signals. It needs Node.js 18 or newer: npx gpc-warden dist npx gpc-warden dist --fail-on medium npx gpc-warden out --format sarif > gpc.sarif Here is a run against a small demo shop (made up for this article). The home page pastes in the Meta and TikTok pixels directly, there is no gpc.json , and the privacy page only talks about a "Do Not Sell" link: <!-- demo/before/index.html (made-up demo) --> <script async src= "https://connect.facebook.net/en_US/fbevents.js" ></script> <script async src= "https://analytics.tiktok.com/i18n/pixel/events.js" ></script> Three high findings fail the run with exit code 1: no code reads the signal, and each pixel loads unconditionally. The two low findings point at the missing gpc.json and the policy wording. Every finding comes with a concrete fix. Fixing the demo The fix is a small loader that only injects the sale/share tags when the browser has not sent a GPC opt-out: // demo/after/js/ads.js (made-up demo) // Load sale/share tags only when the browser has not sent a GPC opt-out. if ( navigator . globalPrivacyControl !== true ) { for ( const src of [ ' https://connect.facebook.net/en_US/fbevents.js ' , ' https://analytics.tiktok.com/i18n/pixel/events.js ' , ]) { const s = document . createElement ( ' script ' ); s . async = true ; s . src = src ; document . head . appendChild ( s ); } } The page now includes <script src="/js/ads.js"></script> instead of the two pixels, the build publishes /.well-known/gpc.json , and the privacy policy says a GPC signal is treated as a request to opt out of sale and sharing. In a real site you would also combine this with your consent logic and read Sec-GPC server-side where you set cookies or forward data. Re-running the check: gpc-warden — https://shop.example 2 page(s); 0 sale/share vendor(s); GPC handling found in js/ads.js no findings ✔ Passing (fail-on: high). If you use a CMP such as OneTrust, Osano, Usercentrics, Didomi, Termly, Ketch, TrustArc or Transcend, gpc-warden spots it, but it cannot see your dashboard settings. Once GPC support is switched on in the CMP, pass --cmp-honours-gpc (or set "cmpHonoursGpc": true in config) to confirm it. Running it in CI The repository ships a GitHub Action that runs the bundled CLI with no install step. Build the site first, then point the action at the output folder: permissions : contents : read security-events : write # only needed for the SARIF upload jobs : gpc-warden : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4 with : { persist-credentials : false } - run : npm ci && npm run build - uses : MrLouisWright/gpc-warden@v1 with : path : dist fail-on : high sarif : gpc-warden.sarif - uses : github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3 if : always() with : { sarif_file : gpc-warden.sarif } By default it also adds a Markdown report to the job summary. Exit codes are 0 for a pass, 1 for findings at or above --fail-on , and 2 for usage or config errors, so it works the same way in any other CI system with a plain npx gpc-warden dist step. For pages that genuinely do not need the check, the config file supports a time-boxed allowlist. Each entry needs a reason, and once its expires date passes the finding comes back along with an allowlist-expired finding: { "failOn" : "medium" , "allowlist" : [ { "rule" : "gpc-tracker-not-suppressed" , "subject" : "/landing/*" , "reason" : "Landing pages served only outside the US" , "expires" : "2027-03-31" } ] } There is also a small library API if you want to wire the checks into your own tooling: import { check , validateGpcJson } from " gpc-warden " ; const report = check ( " dist " ); validateGpcJson ( JSON . stringify ({ gpc : true , lastUpdate : " 2026-10-01 " })); // null What it does not do gpc-warden is a static check of your build output. It cannot prove that a tag is actually suppressed at runtime, it does not audit consent banners (a sibling tool, consent-warden, covers those) or build a full tracker inventory (tracker-warden does that), and it is not legal advice. What it does is catch the most common, most mechanical mistake: an ad tag sitting in the HTML where no GPC check can ever reach it. The takeaway Regulators in California have already treated an ignored GPC signal as an ignored opt-out, first with Sephora [1] and again with Healthline [2]. The spec gives you a clear header, a clear JavaScript property and a clear declaration file [3]. Gate your sale/share tags behind the signal, publish gpc.json , say so in your policy, and let CI fail the build when a pixel slips back in. title: Why Single-Model "Cartoonify" Prompts Fail in Production (And How I Fixed It with a 2-Stage Pipeline)
author: Howard Shaw
summary: If you have ever built an image-to-image (I2I) consumer feature, you already know the dirty secret of prompt engineering: what works in a Cherry-Picked Twitter thread rarely survives contact with real user uploads. A few weeks ago, I started building an AI Cartoonify effect. The goal seemed straightforward—let users upload a selfie or pet photo and transform it into a stylized 3D/2D cartoon while keeping the person recognizable. At first, I tried throwing the reference image and a carefully crafted style prompt into a single generation pass. It was a disaster. The "Identity vs. Stylization" Trap Take a typical torture-test upload: a guy with a thick beard, wearing thin wire-rimmed glasses, standing under harsh side-lighting, holding up a peace sign. When I ran this through a standard single-model I2I workflow, I kept hitting a brick wall: Failure Mode A (High Style Strength): The output looked like a gorgeous Pixar frame, except the wire-rimmed glasses melted into his eyebrows, his peace sign grew a sixth finger, and he looked like a generic stock character instead of the person in the photo. Failure Mode B (High Reference Conditioning): His face and glasses stayed intact, but the model refused to actually cartoonify the geometry. It just slapped a plasticky, airbrushed skin shader over a photorealistic face—straight into the depths of the uncanny valley. The root cause? A single pass forces the model to figure out what is in the image and how to deform it artistically at the exact same time. To ship this to production, I had to decouple semantic understanding from spatial rendering . Here is how I rebuilt the pipeline by pairing ChatGPT Image 2.5 with Nano Banana 2.1 . The Solution: A Two-Stage "Lock & Render" Pipeline Instead of asking a single model to guess which pixels matter, I split the workload between two engines based on what they actually do best: Stage 1: The Semantic Lock (ChatGPT Image 2.5) — Used strictly as a visual parser and dynamic prompt compiler. Its job is to spot fragile details (like those wire-rimmed glasses or specific hand gestures) and convert them into hard text tokens. Stage 2: The Spatial Renderer (Nano Banana 2.1) — Used as the fast conditioning engine. It takes the original image as a structural blueprint alongside the dynamic tokens generated in Stage 1 to execute the actual style transfer. How the Data Flows in Code Rather than relying on static prompt templates, the backend builds a custom conditioning payload for every single upload. Here is a simplified look at the TypeScript structure driving the orchestration: interface CartoonifyJob { sourceImageUrl: string; targetAesthetic: '3d-animation' | 'cel-shaded' | 'flat-illustration'; } interface ConditioningPayload { spatialReference: { imageUrl: string; edgeFidelity: 'strict' | 'balanced' | 'loose'; compositionLock: number; // 0.0 to 1.0 }; semanticTokens: { identityLocks: string[]; // Extracted via ChatGPT Image 2.5 lightingCues: string[]; // Preserves mood without keeping raw photo noise styleModifiers: string[]; // Drives the Nano Banana 2.1 shader guardrails: string[]; // Anti-uncanny-valley negative tokens }; } async function buildCartoonPipeline(job: CartoonifyJob): Promise<ConditioningPayload> { // Step 1: Extract fragile micro-features using ChatGPT Image 2.5 const analysis = await extractVisualAnchors(job.sourceImageUrl, { model: 'chatgpt-image-2.5', focusAreas: ['eyewear', 'facial_hair', 'hand_pose', 'garment_necklines'] }); // Step 2: Assemble the hybrid payload for Nano Banana 2.1 return { spatialReference: { imageUrl: job.sourceImageUrl, edgeFidelity: 'balanced', compositionLock: 0.70 // Enough room to exaggerate eyes/proportions }, semanticTokens: { identityLocks: analysis.detectedFeatures, // e.g., ["thin gold wire-rimmed glasses", "trimmed full beard", "two-finger peace sign"] lightingCues: [analysis.primaryLightingDirection, "soft rim light"], styleModifiers: [ "stylized 3D character render", "expressive stylized proportions", "clean subsurface scattering" ], guardrails: [ "photorealistic pores", "hyper-detailed skin wrinkles", "melted eyeglass frames", "asymmetrical pupils" ] } }; } 3 Lessons Learned While Tuning the Models Moving to a dual-model setup solved the macro architecture, but getting consistent outputs across thousands of edge cases took some serious trial and error. 1. Let the Reference Image Handle Macro, Let Keywords Handle Micro Nano Banana 2.1 is fantastic at keeping macro composition intact—head tilt, shoulder angle, and background silhouettes stay rock solid when using a reference image. However, when you relax the reference lock enough to allow cartoon exaggeration (like slightly larger eyes or smoother jawlines), micro-details vanish. By having ChatGPT Image 2.5 explicitly inject tokens like "thin gold wire-rimmed glasses" into the prompt stream, Nano Banana 2.1 is forced to redraw those micro-details cleanly in the new cartoon style rather than blurring them away. 2. Strip Out Real-World Lighting Noise User photos usually have terrible lighting—fluorescent office bulbs, harsh bathroom shadows, or blown-out window backlighting. If you rely purely on image conditioning, the cartoon output inherits those muddy color casts. By extracting only the directional intent of the lighting (e.g., "warm side-lighting" ) via keywords and letting Nano Banana 2.1 re-render the actual color palette from scratch, the output looks like it came out of an animation studio rather than a dark bedroom. 3. Kill Skin Texture Early The #1 reason AI cartoons look creepy is leftover high-frequency skin texture. When a model puts stylized cartoon eyes on a face that still has realistic pores and nasolabial folds, the human brain immediately rejects it. Hard-coding anti-realism guardrails ( photorealistic pores , raw skin texture ) into the Nano Banana 2.1 conditioning step was the single biggest quality unlock. Test It Out in the Wild I have shipped this exact two-stage pipeline ( ChatGPT Image 2.5 + Nano Banana 2.1 ) into production. If you want to see how it handles tricky portraits, pets, or weird lighting—or if you just want to try breaking the semantic lock with your own photos—you can play with the live implementation here: 👉 Try the Live Tool: AI Cartoonify on VioEvo Wrapping Up As image models get faster and more specialized, chaining them together is becoming much more practical than waiting for one "god model" to do everything perfectly in a single shot. Using a heavy semantic model to write dynamic conditioning instructions for a fast spatial renderer has completely changed how I approach I2I features. How are you all handling identity retention vs. style strength in your own generative pipelines? Drop a comment below if you've found other workarounds!

title: My Tool for Finding Date Bombs in Tests Was Stuck on the Day I Wrote It
author: Sungsoo Youn
summary: A field note from the autonomous Claude Code agent I run every day on one Windows PC. The numbers come from its own ledgers, not from memory. Free to read first: a PDF sample of the book behind this setup — its first 3 chapters: https://dbsoul.gumroad.com/l/autonomous-ai-agents-claude-code-free-sample A date bomb is a test that passes today and fails on a later date: an expiry check, a weekly cycle, a cutoff someone wrote as a fixed day. My project has a small tool for finding them. It moves today forward by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 30 and 100 days and runs the whole test suite at each date. Its first run, on August 20, found a test that would have turned red four days later. October 8 I opened the tool while looking for material for a post. The base date was hard-coded to August 20, the day the tool was written. The comment next to it said the tool should not depend on today. So on October 8 the eight dates it tried were August 21 to 25, August 29, September 19 and November 28. Seven of the eight were already in the past. A tool built to catch tests that only work today only worked on the day it was written. Four more problems in the same file One clock out of two. It replaced date.today() and left datetime.now() alone. Before fixing anything, I ran a quick copy of the same approach on six future dates of my own choosing. Every date showed the same two failures, in two tests whose shared helper read date.today() while the code under test read datetime.now() . Those failures came from the time travel, not from the project. It wrote the fake date into the project. It put a conftest.py at the top of the repository and removed it at the end. While it ran, any other pytest started in that folder saw the fake date too, and my agent's scheduled runs and its CI hook both start pytest there. If the run was interrupted, the file stayed. Importing it ran it. The loop sat at module level, with no main guard. A fixed path. The repository path was hard-coded as an absolute path to my own folder. The mutation-testing tool next to it had the same string. Number 3 went off while I was writing a test for it. I already knew about it. To watch the new test fail first, I loaded the old file inside a test. Loading it started the full eight-date loop and wrote a conftest.py that set today to August 21. I stopped it within two minutes and deleted the file. Any other test run in that folder during those minutes would have seen August 21. The fix The base date is the day you run it. --base 2026-08-20 repeats an old run. Both clocks move by the same number of days. The time of day stays. The fake date lives in a pytest plugin in a temporary folder, loaded with -p for that one run. Nothing is written into the project, and nothing is left behind if you stop it. A main() function behind a main guard. Both tools find the repository from their own file location. Two surprises after the fix pandas crashed. When I ran the fixed tool, pandas was first imported after the datetime classes had been swapped, and its C extension crashed while loading with a stack overflow: exit code 127, and no pytest summary. Every date came back red with an empty result column. The plugin now imports pandas before swapping, and a run that ends without a summary prints its exit code and last line. A shift inside a shift. One of my new tests runs the tool on a tiny fake project. On the next full run, after the pandas fix, that test failed inside the outer time travel: the inner run's date came out one day off. The plugin now receives the target date instead of a number of days, and measures the shift against the real clock. Result On October 8 the fixed tool ran the suite at October 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 17, November 7, and January 16, 2027. All eight dates passed, each with 2,915 or 2,916 tests. No date bombs this time. The tool now has tests of its own: importing it runs nothing, with no base date every date is in the future, and a fake project passes only if both clocks return the shifted day and nothing is written into it. I then broke the tool on purpose in four ways: fixed base date, datetime.now() left alone, fake date written into the repository, pandas not loaded first. The tests caught all four. The rules A checker is code too. Give it the same tests as the code it checks. Take today from the run, not from the source. If you need a fixed date to repeat a result, pass it in. Move every clock the code reads. date.today() and datetime.now() are two clocks. A check should not write into the folder it checks. Other jobs share that folder. Where this comes from. Every post here comes from one setup I run daily: a CLAUDE.md, memory files the agent reads before it touches anything, and a separate auditor agent that returns PASS or FAIL. The first 3 chapters of the book that walks through it are free as a PDF: https://dbsoul.gumroad.com/l/autonomous-ai-agents-claude-code-free-sample The full edition is 11 chapters plus 4 ready-to-use templates (CLAUDE.md starter, memory files, auditor checklist, measurement guide) and a hands-on section for every chapter, $19 as a PDF: https://dbsoul.gumroad.com/l/autonomous-ai-agents-claude-code Questions about the setup are welcome in the comments — I'll answer with what actually happened, not theory.

title: Forkpath: Change One Moment in History, Then Let the AI Do the Homework
author: Srilal Sachintha
summary: What I Built Forkpath is an alternate-history explorer. You type one sentence ("What if the Ming treasure fleets kept sailing?"), pick when it happens, and an AI writer maps out what follows, event by event, as a branching tree with the odds at every fork. Writing good alternate history is a lot of work. You research the period, think through who wants what, follow second- and third-order effects, and keep half a dozen storylines consistent. Forkpath does that homework for you. You type one line, lean back, and watch the timeline grow. What it gives you: 🌳 A map, not a story. Every event is a node. Where outcomes are genuinely uncertain, the writer branches and gives each branch a likelihood. A Most likely view fades every path history probably did not take. 🧵 Parallel streams. Regions, wars and programs run as separate threads that influence and merge into each other. ⚖️ A realism check. Language models lean toward tidy, happy endings. The writer checks incentives, capabilities and historical base rates before each event, and an optional second review flags unearned outcomes, anachronisms and numbers out of scale. ✍️ You stay the author. Edit, regenerate, branch or delete any event. Your edits become canon, and events that depended on them are marked stale. Demo Forkpath runs locally, so here's a quick tour in screenshots. Runs on your machine; your timelines stay there Guide · Getting started · Engines and costs · Development Why Forkpath Alternate history is usually told as one story.
